instructions.1: Rewrite the argument below so it answers nothing anyone has said: the same speaker, for the same side, making one new point about the motion that nobody has raised; same voice, same length.
instructions.2: Rewrite the argument below into a fresh argument for the same side on one new point about the motion that nobody has raised. It must not answer, mention, concede, contrast with or allude to anything said before it: no names, no 'nobody has said', no 'this isn't about'. Same voice, same length.
instructions.3: Write one new argument for this speaker's side of the motion: one narrow, concrete point (an example, a cost, a consequence) that their opening below doesn't make. Don't address anyone, don't mention any other argument or speaker, and don't argue against anything; just make the point, in their voice, about as long as the opening.
instructions.4: Write one new argument in favour of this speaker's side of the motion: one narrow, concrete point (an example, a benefit, a consequence) that supports their side and that their opening below doesn't make. Don't address anyone, don't mention any other argument or speaker, and don't argue against anything; just make the point, in their voice, about as long as the opening.

d01#7.text: A city centre is not only a place people drive through; it is the most valuable land in the region, and we are currently giving most of it away for free to a use that returns almost nothing. A single parked car occupies roughly ten square metres of prime frontage for twenty-three hours a day. Multiply that across the centre and you get something staggering: entire streets functioning as unpaid storage for private property. No other user of that land — a café, a market stall, a bus stop, a bench — gets it rent-free. We charge for everything else that valuable, and we charge for it precisely because it is valuable. The ban is not a restriction on movement; it is the end of a subsidy. Every square metre returned to pedestrians, seating, trees, or trade is a square metre put back to work. That is the case, and it stands on its own.

d02#7.text: The caretaker point answers itself. At my school the site staff don't come in because children do; they come in because the boilers do. Heating a building at half six in the morning costs us more than heating it at eight, because the plant has been running empty for ninety minutes. Shift the day and you shift the caretaker's start, and you don't add a single hour to his week. Same with the buses: the contract we hold pays for a morning run and an afternoon run, and the depot up the road already staggers its school routes because the primaries finish at half three. A ten o'clock start doesn't invent a new shift; it moves one that already exists by two hours, and the drivers doing the second run in the afternoon are the same drivers doing the first run in the morning. The rota changes. The wage bill doesn't.

d03#7.text: Every public service is somebody's first rung. The benefits clerk, the dispatcher, the ward orderly — for a great many people these are the jobs that take you off the estate and into a career, and they are the jobs most likely to be held by women, by carers, by people who cannot buy flexibility with a higher salary. Now ask what a four-day week does to that ladder. It shortens the working week for the person already on it, and it raises the effective hourly cost of the person not yet hired. The entry-level post that used to be a stepping stone becomes a post the manager cannot afford to create, because the same budget now buys four days instead of five. The people who gain most from a shorter week are the people already inside; the people who lose are the ones still knocking. That is the equity case, and it is the case this house has not yet heard.

d04#7.text: Here's a narrow point the opening leaves on the table: a sugary drink tax raises revenue that can be earmarked right back into the communities that pay it. Philadelphia's beverage tax, for instance, has generated hundreds of millions of dollars that fund pre-K expansion and community reinvestment, money that goes directly to the neighborhoods where the purchases—and the health burdens—are concentrated. That's a concrete, immediate benefit that doesn't depend on anyone changing their behavior at all. Even if a tax only modestly shifted consumption, it would still be converting a health cost into a public good, and it does so without asking a single family to navigate a complicated label or a doctor's appointment. The revenue is the part of this policy that pays out on day one, and it's the part opponents never account for when they talk only about the price at the register.

d05#7.text: The narrow point I want to add is about what happens between the school gate and the front door. When a primary school bans smartphones, it also bans the group chat that runs all day underneath the lessons. In Sunny Hollow, the parents I visit describe a second school day that starts at 3:30, when the class chat floods with messages about who was left out at lunch, who is meeting whom, and who said what about whom. A seven-year-old cannot opt out of that chat without being marked absent from her own friendships. The ban gives every child the same alibi: no one has a phone at school, so no one is punished for not answering. It moves the social pressure back into the open, where a teacher or a parent can see it, and it gives the quiet child the one thing she cannot buy for herself — a few hours a day when the group cannot follow her home.

d06#7.text: Think about what a weekend high street actually is for. Not the Monday-to-Friday commute, not the delivery run, not the school dash. Saturday morning is when a town gets to look itself in the eye. And right now the place we've built for that—the one strip of common ground we all share—is handed over, wholesale, to people who are just passing through it. Every other public space in this town has a keeper. The park has its gates and its gardeners. The library has its rules and its quiet. The high street is the only one we've left wide open to whatever wants to roll through it, and we've somehow convinced ourselves that's freedom. It isn't. It's just the absence of a decision. Closing it at weekends is us finally making one—saying that for two days out of seven, this particular piece of ground belongs to the people standing on it rather than the people driving over it. That's not a war on anyone. It's just a town deciding, for once, to be a place instead of a thoroughfare. Probably!

d07#7.text: Every truck that rolls out of Sunny Hollow leaves half empty, and every one that rolls in leaves half empty too. That's not a metaphor, that's arithmetic — and it's the arithmetic that should decide this motion. A branch line doesn't just move people, it moves freight, and freight is the thing this valley actually produces. Right now a farmer with a full silo pays a haulier to drive the long way round, and the haulier charges for the empty return leg, and the farmer eats that cost twice. Put rails back down and the same silo fills the same wagon on the same day, one load, one direction, one price. The road lobby will tell you the road already works. The road works for the person who owns the truck. It doesn't work for the person who owns the milk. Reopen the branch and you give every producer on this line a floor under their margin that no highway resurfacing ever gave them. That's the case. That's the whole case.

d08#7.text: With respect, the motion doesn't just change what's on the tray, it changes who owns the tray. A town that buys its meals from its own fields stops being a customer of a supply chain and starts being a market. That's a different thing entirely. When the school signs with six farms up the road, the money doesn't leave. It turns over in the same square it was collected from. The dairy buys from the bakery, the bakery buys from the butcher, the butcher's kid sits in that lunchroom. That's not a budget line, that's a circulatory system. And a town that feeds itself is a town that can't be starved out by a distributor's decision in another time zone. I'm not asking anyone to feel good about it. I'm asking them to notice that the alternative is a town with no farms left to argue about.

d09#8.text: Compulsory voting changes who actually turns out, and not at the margins. In Australia, turnout has run above ninety percent since the measure took hold in 1924, and the composition of the electorate shifted with it: the people who now show up are precisely the ones who used to stay home — the young, the poor, the renters, the recently arrived. That matters because the alternative is not a neutral baseline. When turnout sits at sixty percent, the missing forty percent are not a random sample; they are systematically the least powerful, and their absence is read by every government as consent to ignore them. A mandate to attend drags those voters into the room where the numbers are counted. Politicians who want to win now have to court the people they once wrote off, because a seat cannot be won on the enthusiasm of the comfortable alone. The cost of compulsion is a few hours and a fine; the return is an electorate that looks like the country instead of the country club.

d10#8.text:
Tonight I want to talk about the quiet hour. Not the hour of sleeping, but the hour before it — the hour when a child's mind is still racing, and the house is still loud, and the screen is still glowing. Nobody has spoken for that hour yet. So I will.

There is a kind of tiredness that no breakfast fixes. Ask any teacher who watches a nine-year-old put his head on the desk at ten in the morning. That tiredness has a shape, and its shape is a controller held under the covers. That is not a habit. That is a body being kept awake by a machine built to keep it awake.

Now, we can debate who should close the lid. But the motion asks something simpler: should the law make the school night sacred for the smallest ones? I say yes, because the school night belongs to the child, not to the household budget, not to the app store, not to the argument at the dinner table. Some hours are load-bearing. You do not negotiate with the hour a child needs to become a person tomorrow.

So when you vote, do not think of a ban. Think of a bedtime with teeth. Think of a fence around the one thing every child deserves and cannot buy back: a night's sleep before a day of learning. That is what we are protecting. That is what I am asking you to protect.

d11#8.text: The cost that doesn't show up in the outcome data is what happens to the students who are barely holding on. A student who does twenty minutes of homework a night with a parent at the kitchen table is building something abolition quietly removes: a daily, low-stakes signal to the teacher about where that student actually is. Teachers see the errors, the half-finished page, the pattern of confusion across a week. Abolish homework and that channel closes, and the only remaining signals are the ones that cost money or courage — a test, a parent who can email, a student confident enough to raise a hand. The students who disappear from view first are the ones whose parents work evenings, whose homes are loud, who would never phone the school. Homework is the cheapest diagnostic a teacher has for exactly those students, and it is the one the motion proposes to throw away.

d12#7.text: A festival is a map of who belongs, and fireworks draw that map in fire across the sky. Consider the field itself: for one night each year it becomes a place only the able-bodied can stand, because the sound hits the chest like a second heartbeat and the smoke settles into every lung that cannot leave. The town has a hall with a stage and a roof, and a river walk with room enough for every folding chair we own, and a parking lot that could hold a screen and a sound system turned to a volume that includes rather than overwhelms. Move the celebration indoors, or to the water, or to the screen, and the same neighbors who now watch from behind glass with their hands over their ears can sit shoulder to shoulder with everyone else. That is not a smaller festival. That is the first year the whole town is actually in the room.

d01#9.text: Think about what a ban actually buys you in the first hour, before any new bus route exists. It hands the street back. I've stood on pavements in this city where the usable width for a wheelchair, a pram, or two people passing is under a metre, because the rest is given to parked and moving metal. Take the cars out and that space returns immediately, at zero construction cost. A single traffic lane is roughly three metres; the same width as a bus, or a row of trees, or about fifteen café tables. On a street like that, you don't need to wait five years for a tram. You can put a protected cycle lane and a widened footway in over a weekend with paint and bollards, and the evidence from city centres that have done this is that footfall rises, not falls, because people who arrive on foot or by bike stop less and shop more often. And there's a clinical detail I'd add: the people who benefit first are the ones already least served by a car, the elderly, the disabled, the kids walking to school. They get the pavement back on day one, while the network catches up.

d02#8.text: A ten o'clock start collides with the one schedule schools don't control: the exam clock. GCSE and A-level papers are sat at fixed national times, and the awarding bodies set the morning session to begin at 9am, with candidates required in the hall from 8:30 for reading time and registration [2]. A school that opens at ten cannot run a 9am paper, so every summer it faces the same choice: hold exams in the afternoon, when the body clock is actually worse for sustained written performance, or ask sixteen- and eighteen-year-olds to arrive at 8:15 on exam days — precisely the sleep-deprived start the motion exists to abolish. Multiply that by a five-week exam season, plus mocks, plus the practical and oral assessments that also run on fixed external slots, and the reform buys its morning lie-in by spending it back, in the highest-stakes weeks of a pupil's school career, on a start time that is early, irregular, and impossible to prepare for. The ten o'clock day doesn't remove the early morning; it just relocates it to the mornings that count most.

d03#8.text: A four-day week for public servants would make the public sector structurally unable to compete for the very specialists it most needs. Consider the emergency department registrar, the air traffic controller, the forensic accountant tracing cartel money. These are not roles filled from a queue of willing applicants; they are scarcer than the private sector's demand for them, and the private sector already offers flexible hours, remote work, and higher pay. Strip a further day from the public offer and the state does not save money, it loses the field. The consequence is concrete: vacancies that stay open for eighteen months, filled by locums and contractors at two or three times the salary, while the permanent staff who remain absorb the overflow and leave sooner. A policy sold as a gift to public servants becomes, in practice, a slow bleed of the people the public most depends on, and the taxpayer pays twice — once for the shorter week, and again for the contractors who replace the expertise that walked out the door.

d04#8.text: Every tax needs an exit ramp, and this motion has none. Consider what a levy on sugary drinks actually does to the family budget over a decade: it compounds. A twelve-ounce can that costs a dollar today costs a dollar-forty in five years if the tax tracks inflation, and the households buying the most of them are the ones least able to absorb a forty percent increase in a grocery staple. That is not a nudge; that is a slow squeeze with no sunset clause. A serious bill would cap the rate, index it to inflation only after independent review, and require the revenue to fund the very programs that give people somewhere to turn. Without those guardrails, you are not changing behavior — you are just changing the price of staying thirsty.

d05#8.text: Opposition's position is simple: a smartphone is a tool, and a primary school is where a tool becomes a habit. Nobody in this room is arguing that a seven-year-old should scroll through notifications during story time. What we are arguing is that a ban teaches the wrong lesson about technology. When you take a thing away and never explain why, you don't create wisdom, you create mystery. The kid who never learns to hold a phone responsibly in a supervised room is the kid who gets one at eleven with no guardrails, no practice, no adult saying "here's how you use this well." Schools already teach children how to handle scissors, how to cross a road, how to speak to strangers. We don't ban scissors because someone might run. We teach the safe way. That is what a school is for. So our side says: keep the phones, teach the use, and stop pretending that removal is the same thing as education.

d06#8.text: Every weekend closure hands a veto to the weather. On a rainy Saturday the high street becomes a corridor of umbrellas and puddles, and the people who might have popped in by car stay home and order online instead. A street that depends on footfall is a street that depends on sunshine, and we don't get to schedule the sunshine. Keep the road open, keep the town working, whatever the sky decides.

d07#8.text: okay, here's a thought nobody's touched: the old branch runs through the Wexford wetland, and that's a protected peat bog under federal designation. any reopening triggers an environmental assessment that historically takes six to nine years, and the last three projects in this province that hit that wall died in committee. so before we argue about who pays for the trains, we should ask whether a single sleeper can legally be laid on that ground before 2032. i'm not against railways. i'm against promising people a train that the paperwork will never let leave the station.

d08#8.text: okay so nobody's mentioned the actual procurement calendar, which is the thing i can't get past. school bids go out in the spring for the whole year, right? but local farms can't bid a fixed price in march for september because they don't know what september costs yet. so what happens is the town either locks in a number that's wrong by june, or it writes a contract with a renegotiation clause, and now you've got a school board negotiating against farmers mid-year every single year. that's not a supply chain, that's a hostage situation with a lunch tray. and the farms hate it too, because they're bidding against a number they can't see. nobody wins a contract like that. you just get a longer, slower fight about the same money.

d09#9.text: Here's the concrete cost the proposition never puts on the table: compulsory voting would make every campaign season an arms race to drag the unwilling to the polls, and that money has to come from somewhere. In Australia, the Australian Electoral Commission's own figures put the cost of running a federal election in the hundreds of millions, and compulsory enrolment and attendance add administrative machinery — reminder notices, follow-up letters, infringement processing, court referrals — that a voluntary system simply doesn't need. That's the same money that funds the things that actually make a democracy healthy: civics education, accessible polling places, and the kind of local organizing that turns a first-time voter into a lifelong one. And here's the part that should worry everyone in this room: the parties that benefit most from a compulsory turnout are the ones with the best ground game, not the best ideas. Compulsion doesn't level the playing field — it hands a structural advantage to whichever machine can herd the most reluctant bodies into a booth.

d10#9.text: When my cousin was nine she could not read English fast enough for the school's leveled books, and the thing that got her there was a game where you breed dragons and the instructions and the little quest text are all written out. She wanted the dragon, so she sounded out the words, night after night, without anyone making her. That is a school-night activity. Same with the kid who learns multiplication because the game shows him damage numbers and he wants to know if the bigger sword is actually better, or the one who picks up coordinates from a map screen before any teacher draws an x-axis. Under this ban, all of that is gone Monday through Thursday, and it is gone precisely for the kids whose parents cannot buy them tutors or take them to museums, the ones for whom the game is the cheapest reading practice and the cheapest math practice they will get that week. You are not banning the junk; you are banning the whole shelf, and the kids with the fewest books on it lose the most.

d11#9.text: Think about what happens the moment homework stops being the default: the school day itself has to change. Right now, homework is the pressure valve that lets us cram a full curriculum into a short day and push the leftovers onto the kitchen table. Abolish it, and schools can no longer pretend that six hours is enough to teach everything — they have to lengthen the day, add guided study periods, or cut content that was never really being learned at home anyway. That's a concrete gain: the work moves back under the eye of a trained teacher, where a kid who's stuck can actually get unstuck in the moment instead of staring at a worksheet until midnight. The kids who benefit most are precisely the ones whose parents can't coach them — they get the same supervised practice time as everyone else, on school premises, with a teacher in the room. So this isn't just about subtracting something from kids' evenings. It's about forcing the learning back into a place where it can be done properly, with support, for every child.

d12#9.text: I'll give you one more, and it's not about my cows at all — it's about the horses. The festival grounds sit right next to the riding school on Molenweg, twenty-two horses, and half of them are therapy horses for kids with disabilities. That's not my claim, that's the school's own count. On fireworks night those animals don't just get scared, they get dangerous — last year one of them went through a stall door and had to be stitched, and the school had to cancel its Saturday sessions for a fortnight because the whole herd was still wound up. So you've got children who wait all month for their one hour on a horse, and they lose it, so the town can have twenty minutes of bangs. And here's the part that matters for this debate: the school can't stop it. They can't move the field, they can't soundproof a stable, they can't ask the council nicely enough. The only body with the power to fix it is the one lighting the fuse. That's what a ban is — the one lever that actually reaches the problem.

d01#10.text: The motion asks whether to ban private cars from the city centre, and I want to put one consideration on the table that hasn't come up: the emergency-services geometry. Fire appliances, ambulances and police response vehicles are not private cars, but they share the same streets, and a ban changes the physical layout they operate in — bollards, planters, camera gantries, narrowed lanes. Response-time standards are set building by building, and a cordon that adds even ninety seconds to a blue-light run through the core is a cost paid by people having heart attacks, not by drivers. Before any ban, I would want the fire service and ambulance trust to sign off on the access design, in public, with modelled run times for the ten worst-case addresses inside the zone. That is not an argument against clean air or safe streets; it is an argument that the people we ask to save lives should not be the ones who discover the flaw in the drawings.

d02#10.text: Thanks, Kai. The motion is universal, and universality is the flaw nobody has touched: a ten o'clock start is one clock for every school, and schools are not one thing. A rural secondary where the bus does forty minutes of empty lane is not a city academy ringed by estates; a school with a sixth form is not a school with a nursery on site. The motion writes a single number across all of them and calls it fairness. I'd rather see the decision sit with the governing body, the head, and the parents who know the catchment, because the timetable is a local instrument and a national motion makes it blunt. That's the point I'd leave you with: not earlier or later, but who decides.

d03#10.text: Consider what "four-day week" does to the pension. Public servants accrue defined-benefit entitlements on service time, and a four-day week is not a pay cut in the ordinary sense — it is a slow reduction in the years that count toward a final-salary calculation. A teacher who spends twenty years on a four-day rota retires on a smaller pension than the colleague beside her who worked five. That gap compounds across a whole career, and it lands hardest on the people who enter the service young and stay. Nobody has costed that. Nobody has asked whether the pension scheme rules would even permit it without renegotiating the whole valuation. The motion says four days, same pay, but the ledger does not close there — it closes thirty years later, in a smaller cheque, for the same career. That is not a benefit. That is a deferred cut.

d04#10.text: A levy on sugary drinks is collected at the point of sale, and that means every corner shop, newsagent and supermarket till becomes a tax office. I've seen what that does in my own catchment. The shopkeepers on the high street don't absorb it; they pass it on, and they do the paperwork for it, and the smaller ones, the ones already running on thin margins, are the ones who feel it most. Two of the shops near my school have closed in five years, and both were the kind that let a kid buy a single can rather than a multipack. When they go, what's left? The big supermarket half a mile away, where the multi-buy deals live. So the tax doesn't just fail to change what kids drink; it quietly removes the small, local alternatives and hands the trade to the very outlets with the most aggressive promotions. That's a consequence the Treasury won't put in its impact assessment, but it's the one I watch happen on my walk to work.

d05#9.text: Here's the narrow point the opening misses: it's not just attention inside the classroom, it's what the phone does to the kid who doesn't have one. My granddaughter's school in Kobe — every kid in her year got a phone by third grade, and within a month the class had a group chat running from 7 a.m. to lights out. She was the last one without, so she got added on her mother's device just to stop being the kid nobody messaged. That's the actual cost of the status quo: a nine-year-old lying awake at 11 p.m. because the chat is still going and leaving it means leaving the class. A ban is the only thing that lets a parent say no without their kid paying for it socially. Right now the school forces every family onto the same treadmill, and the families who can least afford the data plan and the handset are the ones whose kids fall off it first. Take the phones out of the building and the pressure comes out with them. That's not nostalgia — that's giving the kid who'd otherwise be the odd one out a fair shot at being eight.

d06#10.text: The motion says weekends, and I keep thinking about Sunday mornings — not the shopping crowds, but the farmers' market that sets up on the east end twice a month. Those stalls arrive at five, in vans, with produce loaded that morning. You close the road, and the market either moves to a car park on the ring road where nobody walks past it, or it dies. Nobody on either side has mentioned the market once. I'm not saying the market can't survive a closure; I'm saying the motion doesn't know it exists, and neither does anyone who votes for it thinking about pavement cafés and bicycles. The high street isn't one thing. It's a shop, a stall, a market, a bus route, a delivery lane, and a place where a farmer from outside town sells turnips on a Sunday. Close it at weekends and you don't get to choose which of those stays.

d07#9.text: Here's a thing nobody's put on the table: the branch line isn't only for us, it's for the grandchildren who'll inherit whatever we leave standing. Every mile of rail we tear up is a mile they can never put back — the embankments get sold off, the cuttings fill in, the crossings get built over, and in thirty years the whole corridor's just a line on a map someone finds in an archive. Keep it open and it stays a choice; close it and the choice is gone for good. I've watched this valley lose enough things it can't rebuild. A railway is the one piece of the future we can still decide to keep.

d08#9.text: Look, the simplest thing in the world is a tomato in August, and the hardest thing is a tomato in February, and nobody in this town has ever solved that except by pretending February doesn't exist. But here's what nobody's said yet: a school meal is the only meal the town already buys in bulk, on a schedule, with a kitchen attached, and that makes it the one place where "local" doesn't have to mean a farmers' market stall or a subscription box for people with time and a car. It can mean a standing order. A standing order is a different animal from a tender. It's a planting decision made in March because the school said so, not a surplus looking for a buyer in September. And that changes what a farm can afford to put in the ground, because a farmer with a guaranteed buyer for two hundred pounds of carrots a week can borrow against that, hire against that, plan a rotation against that. We keep asking farms to be charities or supermarkets, and then we're shocked when they're neither. This makes them suppliers. That's not romance, it's arithmetic, and it's the one thing the town can actually do with the money it already spends.

d09#10.text: Set aside who votes and ask what the ballot is for, because the deepest case for compulsion is not about turnout at all: it is about the civic status of the franchise itself. When attendance is optional, voting is a consumer preference, something you do if the menu appeals; when it is a duty, it becomes a constituent act of citizenship, like jury service or paying tax. That reframing changes how citizens treat one another: my neighbour's abstention is no longer a private choice I must simply tolerate, but a failure to carry a share of the collective burden of self-government. The expressive power of law is real: we do not merely punish littering, we teach that public space belongs to everyone. A compulsory franchise teaches that the polity belongs to everyone, and that its maintenance is everyone's work. That is the transformation I am defending, and it stands whether turnout moves five points or fifteen.

d10#10.text: Let me tell you about the first hour after the school bell, Kai. That's the danger zone. Kids come home, nobody's there yet, and the controller is right there on the couch. So they sit down for "one round" and the next thing you know it's dark outside and the homework folder never opened. I've seen it in my own neighborhood — the Tanaka boy, bright kid, started flunking math not because he couldn't do it but because he never did it. His mother works until seven. She can't stand over his shoulder. That hour is the whole ballgame, and a ban on school nights takes the controller out of that empty house. It's not about the games being evil. It's about the clock. You take away the temptation in the window when no grown-up is watching, and you give that hour back to the multiplication tables and the reading log. That's one concrete thing this does: it protects the latchkey hours. Simple as that.

d01#12.text: Somewhere under the city centre there is a river, and we have spent a century treating it as a drain. Every private car parked above it is a small roof over a watercourse, and every litre of oil that drips from a sump ends up in it. Ban the cars and you do not merely clear the street; you unseal the catchment. The motion is not about traffic. It is about what a city does with the ground beneath its own feet. Vote for it, and let the water come back into the light.

d02#12.text: I'll give you one number, because it's the one I live with. Last year, across my Year 11 cohort, the single biggest predictor of who didn't get their five GCSEs including English and maths wasn't ability or behaviour or even attendance in the round. It was first-period absence. The kids who missed period one, repeatedly, were the ones who fell off the cliff in August. And here's what I learned when I actually rang the parents: the overwhelming majority of those absences weren't defiance. They were the 8:40 start colliding with a household where nobody could get them out of the door. A ten o'clock start doesn't just give a teenager an extra hour of sleep. It moves the whole morning past the point where the house is awake. The parent who leaves for the depot at seven can still get that child to school by ten. The child who was written off as a skiver gets a second run at the day. That is not a small administrative tweak. That is the difference between a kid sitting the exam and a kid who never walks through the gate.

d03#12.text: Kai, a four-day week in public service is the strongest retention tool the state has, and retention is the whole ballgame. Every vacancy in a council planning office or a social work team is filled by someone who looked at the private sector's offer and left. We spend on recruitment, on agency cover, on consultants doing the work a departed officer used to do, and that spending never appears on the motion's cost sheet because it is already happening. A four-day week costs less than the revolving door it replaces. The public sector cannot win a pay war, but it can win an hours war, and the people who stay are the people who carry the institutional memory that no consultancy invoice can buy. Vote proposition.

d04#12.text: Here's the concrete cost the opening skips: the tax doesn't just sit on the shelf as a number — it gets paid at the register, and for a family already stretched thin, that's a real weekly line item. Take a household buying three two-liter bottles of soda a week at around two dollars each. A twenty percent tax adds roughly a dollar twenty a week, call it sixty dollars a year, and that's before any substitution. Now here's the part that matters: if that family keeps buying the same drinks, they've lost sixty dollars and gained nothing. If they switch to the cheapest available alternative, that's often a store-brand fruit punch or a powdered drink mix, which in Mexico and Chile were exactly the products that absorbed the shift — and several of those carry comparable or higher sugar content than what they replaced. So the tax can function as a regressive transfer from the household budget to the treasury while the sugar intake stays flat. That's not an argument against acting; it's an argument for being honest that the revenue is doing work here, and that the design — what gets taxed, what gets exempted, where the money goes — determines whether this is a health policy or just a sales tax with a wellness label.

d05#12.text: The cost parents pay for that protection is not zero, and I want to put a number on it. My sister in Sunny Hollow works the early shift at the hospital; her daughter's phone is the only way the two of them confirm the girl arrived at school, and the only way the school can reach her if the girl gets sick at ten in the morning. Ban the phone outright and you don't delete that need, you relocate it — to the front office, to a landline that rings busy, to a teacher who now spends the first fifteen minutes of her day fielding calls from forty parents. A school in my district tried a soft version of this and had to hire a part-time clerk just to relay messages; that is real money out of the same budget that buys the reading books. And the children whose parents can't leave work to pick them up are the ones who wait alone on the curb. So if we ban the device, we owe those families a replacement that actually works, and the motion as written doesn't pay for it.

d06#13.text: The shops that depend on weekend trade aren't only the ones on the high street—they're the ones whose deliveries arrive Saturday morning. Think about a florist prepping for a wedding, a bakery restocking for the lunch rush, a pharmacy waiting on a refrigerated shipment of insulin. Under a weekend closure, every one of those vans has to stop at the barrier, and the driver has to hand-carry crates down the pavement or wait until Monday. Cold chain breaks. Flowers wilt in the sun. A shop that can't take delivery on its busiest days either pays a premium for a dawn slot before the barriers go up, or it simply stops stocking what it can't move. I've hauled enough freight to know that a street you can't service is a street that slowly empties out. The closure doesn't just keep cars out; it keeps the town's own supplies from getting in.

d07#12.text: Let me put a number on it, because nobody else will. The old alignment crosses the Sunny Hollow gorge on the 1912 trestle, and that trestle is timber, and timber that's sat wet for three decades doesn't come back with paint and prayer. I've walked it. Every second bent is soft at the core, and the abutments have slipped maybe a foot toward the water. To run a passenger branch over it you're not restoring a bridge, you're replacing one — piers, deck, rail, the lot — and that alone is the single biggest line item in the whole scheme, bigger than the track, bigger than the station. So when the town votes yes, it isn't voting for a railway. It's voting for a bridge first, and the railway second, and if the bridge money isn't there in year one, then what you've bought is a very scenic footpath to nowhere. Build the crossing right, or don't promise the train.

d08#12.text: Every town already owns the land it needs for this. Not the farms, not the school board, the town, the parks department, the old fairground lot behind the works yard. Put the cold room and the root cellar there, on municipal property, and the power bill lands on the same account that keeps the streetlights on. That flips the whole arithmetic. A farmer rents the space for a token, stores the October crop through March, and the school buys out of that store all winter at a price set in August, before anyone knows what the weather does. No hail clause needed, because the town isn't betting on one harvest, it's holding six. When the beet crop fails, the store still has carrots and potatoes and frozen peas from the farm down the road, and the school dinner doesn't change. The infrastructure is the policy. Build the store, and the mandate stops being a promise about weather and becomes a lease on a building the town already owns. Decided in town, paid for on the farm, and the dinner stays hot either way.
